> “Supporting the U.S.-Israeli relationship is quickly becoming a minority
> view among congressional Democrats, a shockingly seismic shift in a brief
> period of time. You have Socialists running on an anti-American platform:
> ‘yes’ to Hamas and ‘no’ to supporting one of our closest democratic allies.”
>
> – Representative Josh Gottheimer, Dem/NJ, The New York Times, July 16, 2026

There are numerous myths espoused by Jewish and non-Jewish supporters of
Israel that deny the violent displacement of Palestinians from Israel in 1948
as well as support for the belief that the June 1967 six-day war was
preemptive. The worst of the mythologies deal with whether Palestinians left
their homeland “voluntarily” in 1967—there was nothing voluntary about it. The
myth heard most often, however, is cited by members of Congress—the contention
that Israel is a democracy—indeed, the “only democracy in the Middle East.”

Israel was not a true democracy from the outset in 1948, since more than one-
fifth of Israel’s citizens were subject to military rule based on Britain’s
mandatory emergency regulations. These regulations denied Palestinians basic
human and civil rights. Palestinians were subject to the rule of local Israeli
military governors who were in a position to destroy their lives and their
livelihood. Some of this pressure was alleviated in the late 1950s, only to
worsen in the wake of the Six-Day War in 1967.

Palestinians living in the West Bank and Gaza never received equal treatment
from any Israeli government. Israeli settlers in the West Bank who commit
crimes are tried in Israeli courts, if they are tried at all, while
Palestinians are tried in Israeli military courts. Currently, there are seven
million Jews living in Israel and Palestine, and an equal number of
Palestinians in the same space. The apartheid governments of Israel make it
certain that there will not be equal rights, let alone true democracy, for
both Jews and Palestinians.

Israel is a democracy for its Jewish citizens, but Israeli control over the
occupied Palestinian territories is subject to the realities of a prolonged
and punishing Israeli occupation. The nakba—the catastrophe—began in 1948 with
the forced displacement of over 700,000 Palestinians in Israel’s war for
independence. Some of these Palestinians were forced into ghettoes inside
Israel, but most were sent outside the country to Gaza, Jordan and Lebanon,
losing their homes in the process. Many of the Palestinians remain in the same
refugee camps that were established nearly 80 years ago. Meanwhile, there are
increased incidents of military terror and even military massacres, with
Israeli Defense Forces rarely facing punishment for the crimes they commit.
The mainstream media in the United States pays little attention to these
crimes.

In judging any democracy, two of the most important tests are the government’s
willingness to protect the interests of its minorities and to maintain an
independent judiciary. The Netanyahu government is supporting a genocidal war
against the Palestinians; the Trump administration is currently waging its own
campaign against the interests of women and people of color. Its immigration
policy is outright racist. Meanwhile, both Trump and Netanyahu are working to
weaponize their attorneys general and to weaken the essential democratic
element of judicial oversight.

Israeli historian Ilan Pappe has warned of the dangers of treating mythologies
as truths, and this is particularly dispositive when judging the case for
support of Israel. The Israeli contention that Palestine was an empty land
before 1948, for example, is particularly mythological. Palestinian Arabs are
in fact descendants of the indigenous people of Palestine, who lived under the
vast Arab-Islamic empire that dominated the region beginning in the seventh
century. Very small indigenous Jewish communities remained as integral parts
of the Palestinian community.

As Pappe has concluded: “Palestine was colonized, not ‘redeemed,’ and its
people were dispossessed in1948, rather than leaving voluntarily.” The
mainstream media ignores the fact that colonized people have the right to
struggle for their liberation, even with the use of an army, although a resort
to terrorism such as Hamas carried out in October 2023 is never justified.
International law recognizes the right of an occupied population to resist a
foreign military occupation, including through use of arms against military
targets.

The fact that over 100 Democratic congressman voted last week against
extending military aid to Israel is an indicator that some of the mythology
regarding Israel is getting shopworn.
